title: Lior and the Inheritance
premise: Bram Winterbourne, archivist of St. Aldhelm's Cathedral, receives two anonymous letters: one confessing to a murder committed the night the crypt was sealed five years ago, and one promising a second confession if Bram can find 'the ledger that hides in daylight.' Following the clues through baptismal records, funeral accounts, and marginalia, Bram discovers the crypt's lock was changed the same week the town's beloved benefactor, Edith Marlowe, died — and that her fortune, which saved the cathedral and half the town, was built on a death her heirs have been paying to keep buried. The confessing letter-writer is Edith's gardener, dying of cancer and seeking absolution; the second letter comes from her grandson, who wants Bram silenced. In the climax, Bram opens the crypt during the midnight service, forcing the family's confession before the whole congregation, and must choose between exposing the inheritance that keeps the town alive or preserving the lie that has become its foundation.
about_author: Yara Eastwick is a former parish records clerk from the English coast who spent a decade cataloguing documents no one was meant to read twice. Her mysteries are known for their quiet dread, ecclesiastical settings, and villains who believe they are the heroes.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Hand
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. On an ordinary Tuesday, two letters arrive in identical handwriting: one confesses to a killing inside the locked crypt five years ago; the other promises 'the rest' if Bram finds what hides in plain sight. The emotional beat is unease — Bram's ordered world develops its first crack.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Establishing the cathedral archive, its routines, and the town of Wetherholt's dependence on the late Edith Marlowe's bequest. Bram quietly checks the crypt seal and finds the lock was replaced the week she died. Beat: curiosity sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Gardener Knew
chapters.summary: Bram visits Silas Crane, the Marlowes' elderly former gardener, ostensibly about grounds records. Silas is gaunt, newly ill, and flinches at the word 'crypt.' He gives nothing away but presses a pressed flower — edelweiss — into Bram's hand. Beat: first human cost glimpsed.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, night work. The clue resolves: the cathedral's public donor ledger lists gifts whose amounts encode dates and initials. The final entry before the crypt sealed reads E.M. — £1,947. Bram realizes it points to a person, not money. Beat: the thrill of decoding curdles into dread.

chapters.title: The Grandson Arrives
chapters.summary: Julian Marlowe's POV. Edith's grandson returns to Wetherholt as chair of the restoration fund, charming the town council. Privately he burns a box of his grandmother's correspondence and asks pointed questions about the archive. Beat: the antagonist revealed to the reader, hidden from Bram.

chapters.title: A Confession Half-Finished
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A third letter arrives, mid-sentence, unsigned: 'She asked me to help carry him down and I did, God forgive me, I did—' The handwriting matches both originals. Bram begins keeping a private file outside the archive. Beat: complicity begins; Bram is now hiding something too.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Buried
chapters.summary: Bram cross-references burial registers against sexton logs and finds a gap: Thomas Renner, verger, listed as 'departed for Canada' in the same week — though his sister never received a letter. Beat: grief on behalf of a stranger; the mystery gains a face.

chapters.title: Tea with the Widow Renner
chapters.summary: Alternating Bram and Agnes Renner's POVs. Agnes, sharp and unfooled, admits she always suspected Thomas never left. She gives Bram his last unsent letter home, which mentions 'the lady's night business.' Beat: alliance formed across class lines; stakes become personal.

chapters.title: Restoration Fund
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian pressures the bishop to restrict archive access, framing it as security. He offers Bram a generous consultancy fee. Bram declines, and both understand what that means. Beat: open hostility beneath civility; power flexing.

chapters.title: The Night Business
chapters.summary: Bram reconstructs the encoded ledger fully: repeated payments to Silas dated the nights Edith's ledgers were 'audited.' Thomas Renner found them. The sequence implies Edith alive, present, complicit — or being protected. Beat: moral vertigo; the victim may have been the architect.

chapters.title: Silas Breaks
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Dying, Silas summons Bram and tells part of it: Thomas fell during a confrontation over the ledgers; Edith ordered the crypt sealed 'until God decides'; Silas carried the body down because he loved her. He refuses to say whether it was murder. Beat: confession without absolution.

chapters.title: The Lock That Changed
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram obtains the locksmith's old invoice: Julian, then nineteen, collected the new crypt key the morning after Thomas vanished. Either Julian obeyed his grandmother — or acted alone. Beat: suspicion pivots; the heir's alibi is his own grief.

chapters.title: Fire in the Archive
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A small fire damages the record room; Bram's private file survives only because he broke protocol and took it home. The bishop suspends him pending inquiry. Beat: isolation — the investigator becomes the suspect, and the institution closes ranks.

chapters.title: Agnes at the Door
chapters.summary: Agnes's POV. Agnes shelters Bram, and they compare notes: she remembers Julian's car idling by the crypt gate that week. Bram admits he is no longer sure he wants the truth if it destroys the fund that pays the town's wages. Beat: theme crystallized — the price of survival.

chapters.title: The Second Promise
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian confronts Bram privately, offering truth-for-silence: he'll confess everything after the restoration gala, once the endowment is legally untouchable. Bram sees the trap — a confession no court can touch, delivered to a town that can't afford to hear it. Beat: temptation offered in good faith.

chapters.title: Edelweiss
chapters.summary: Bram traces the flower: Edith grew edelweiss in the walled garden, and a fresh cutting sits on Silas's sill — someone still tends it. Watching the garden at night, Bram sees Julian kneeling there, weeding, talking to the grave-shaped flowerbed. Beat: unexpected tenderness toward the antagonist.

chapters.title: The Midnight Service
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. At the anniversary vigil, Bram uses his suspended-but-not-revoked keys to unlock the crypt during the service, inviting the congregation to witness 'what we have all been paying for.' Julian moves to stop him; Silas, wheeled in by Agnes, says 'Let him.' Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: What Lies Below
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. By candlelight the town sees Thomas Renner's coffin, unregistered, and the ledger pages lining it like shroud — Edith's order: bury the evidence with the man. Bram reads the amounts aloud; the arithmetic of the town's survival is laid bare. Beat: horror and pity entwined.

chapters.title: The Whole Confession
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Before the congregation, Julian confesses: Thomas came to blackmail Edith over embezzled funds; in the struggle Thomas fell; Edith made Julian swear silence to protect three hundred jobs, then died leaving him the burden. Whether it was murder, even Julian no longer knows. Beat: catharsis without clean answers.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Legal aftermath: manslaughter charges considered, the fund frozen, the town furious at Bram for the truth and at Julian for the lie. Agnes forgives Julian; some neighbors never forgive Bram. Silas dies peacefully, having confessed. Beat: the cost of truth itemized.

chapters.title: The Ledger, Rewritten
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Reinstated, Bram re-catalogues the archive honestly, including a new public ledger naming Thomas Renner among the cathedral's dead. The town votes to keep the endowment under independent trustees rather than dissolve it. Beat: imperfect repair; identity rebuilt around integrity.

chapters.title: A Letter of My Own
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, closing. A year later, Bram writes a letter to Thomas Renner's memory and seals it in the reopened crypt — a confession of their own: that knowing felt like duty until it felt like hunger. The last line mirrors the first letter: 'I confess I would do it again.' Beat: quiet, earned resolution.
